title: The house with the katsura tree
translation: A woman was living in a run-down house that nobody visited. It was a time when she had to keep away from people, and she stayed shut in, with nothing to do. A man decided to go and see her. He went secretly, in the dim light of the early evening moon. A dog made a great fuss, a maid came out and asked, "Who's there?", and he had her announce him and went straight in.

The place looked so forlorn that it hurt to see it. How did she get by here? He stood for a while on the rough wooden floor. Then a calm, young voice said, "In here," and he went in through a sliding door that stuck in its groove.

Inside, it wasn't so dreary. It was tasteful. The lamp was far off and dim, but he could see the gleam of nice things, and there was a scent that hadn't just been put on for him. It felt lived in, and welcoming. "Lock the gate properly," someone said. "It might rain. Put the carriage under the gateway, and find places for his people." "Looks like we'll get a proper sleep tonight," the servants whispered. They kept their voices down, but the house was small, and he could just hear them.

He told her everything that had happened lately, in detail, and the first cock crowed in the middle of the night. They went on talking, seriously, about the past and the future, until the cocks crowed again, loud and bright, over and over. Was it getting light? But this was not a house you had to slip out of before dawn, so he stayed a little longer. When the cracks in the shutters turned white, he told her he would never forget this, and left.

It was early summer. The treetops and the garden had all turned a fresh green, and the dawn was lovely. He still remembers it. They say that whenever he passes that way, he keeps looking back at the big katsura tree until it's out of sight.

literal: In a run-down house where no one came, a woman, at a time when she had something to keep away from, was staying shut in with nothing to do;
a certain person, meaning to visit her, came secretly to call at a time when the evening moon was dim,
(and) when a dog challenged him loudly, a maid came out and said 'Where are you from?', and he had her announce him at once and went in.
The forlorn state of the place: how can she live here? It is very painful (to see).
While he stood for a while on the poor wooden floor, there was someone who, with a calm and youthful air, said 'This way', so he went in through a sliding door that looked hard to open and close.

The state inside was not very dreary; it was tasteful, the lamp was dim over there, but the gleam of things could be seen, and with a scent that was not sudden, she had made the place very homely to live in.
When (she) said, 'Lock the gate well. It may rain; the carriage under the gate, the attendants here and there',
(the servants) whispered, 'Tonight it seems we can sleep at ease'; though they kept it quiet, the place was small, so it could faintly be heard.
Then, while he was telling her in detail about the things of recent days, the cock of the deep night crowed.
In earnest talk reaching over past and future, this time the cocks too crowed again and again in bright voices, so he wondered if it was getting light, but
since it was not the kind of place where one must hurry (away) in the deep of night, he relaxed a little, and when the gaps turned white, he said things that are hard to forget and went out;

remembering the dawn of about the fourth month, when the treetops and the garden had all turned wonderfully green, and it was graceful and lovely, even now he watches until the big katsura tree is hidden, they say.

notes.quote: 女の憚る事あるころにて
notes.text: 'A time when she had something to avoid': probably mourning, or a period of ritual seclusion ({物忌|ものいみ}) when she was not supposed to see visitors. Commentators differ. Either way, she is alone, and the visit is secret.

notes.quote: ある人とぶらひ給はむとて
notes.text: The man is never named. The text uses honorific verbs for him all the way through ({給|たま}ふ, おはす), so he is someone of high rank. The neglected house, the barking dog and the visit by evening moonlight are stock scenes of Heian court tales such as the Tale of Genji, and the long, unbroken sentences copy their style.
{夕月夜|ゆふづくよ}: the moon early in the month, which is already up at dusk and sets soon after. Dim light, and not for long.

notes.quote: 俄にしもあらぬにほひ
notes.text: A scent that was 'not sudden': incense that had soaked into the house over time, not something burned quickly because a visitor came (on incense in clothes, see section 8).
もぞ: 'it might (and that would be bad)', a worry about something unwelcome. A practical reason for the guests to stay the night.

notes.quote: 今宵ぞやすきいは寝べかめる
notes.text: Probably the man's attendants: if their master stays the night, they can sleep too. Some commentators give the words to the women of the house instead. いは{寝|ね}: 'sleep', an old poetic word. べかめる: べかる + めり, 'it seems we can'.
Lovers in old Japanese poetry part at cockcrow, and the first crow, in the dark, is the warning. Here the second, brighter crowing comes too, and he still does not have to leave.
{卯月|うづき}: the fourth month of the old calendar, roughly May, the first month of summer.

notes.quote: 今も見おくり給ふとぞ
notes.text: とぞ: 'so they say', with いふ left out. The story ends as hearsay, and in the present tense: he still looks back. {桂|かつら}: the katsura tree, a large tree with heart-shaped leaves, here apparently growing at her house.
